profile.purpose: A step-by-step tutorial on re-waxing a Barbour waxed cotton jacket so it looks factory-fresh rather than sticky or shiny, demonstrated on a friend's worn jacket.
profile.thesis: Re-waxing a Barbour is easier and looks better if you work somewhere hot, blow-dry the wax in while blotting the excess with paper towels, and spread the wax with a paper towel instead of a sponge.
key_takeaways: You need Barbour Thornproof Dressing, a way to heat water, a hair dryer and plenty of paper towels; a sponge is optional and he recommends against it.
Melt the tin of wax in hot water, but watch out: the tin can tip over and spill.
Work in as hot a room as possible, because the wax dries almost immediately in a cool room.
Never machine-wash a waxed jacket. The factory wax is pressed into the fabric before stitching, so re-waxing only adds a second layer on top.
Blow-drying melts the wax into the fibres. Blotting with a paper towel while blow-drying removes excess wax for a matte, non-greasy finish.
Spills and over-waxing can be fixed by melting the wax with the hair dryer and blotting it up with paper towel.
A paper towel spreads the wax faster and more easily than a sponge, which soaks the wax back up.

outline.title: Introduction to jacket
outline.summary: Michael introduces the tutorial on waxing a Barbour jacket so it looks new rather than re-waxed, and previews fixing spills and the trick that made the job easier.

outline.title: Jacket inspection
outline.summary: A look at Christian Cerrone's roughly three-year-old Barbour, with patches where the wax has worn off and nicely aged buttons.

outline.title: Materials and setup
outline.summary: The supplies needed: sponge, a way to heat water, the tin of Thornproof Dressing (which tips over and spills), a hair dryer and paper towels.

outline.title: Waxing process
outline.summary: The basic steps: lay the jacket flat on a protected surface, melt the wax tin in hot water, and rub the wax on, working somewhere as hot as possible because it dries fast.

outline.title: Heating and finishing
outline.summary: Why you can't machine-wash a waxed jacket or match the factory wax, and how to blow-dry the wax in while blotting with paper towel for a dry, matte finish that puts looks ahead of water resistance.

outline.title: Fixing mistakes and results
outline.summary: After spilling about a third of the tin on the jacket, he melted and blotted the excess with paper towel until it blended in, showing that over-waxing can be fixed.

outline.title: An anecdote and tips
outline.summary: Don't use a sponge, which soaks the wax back up. A wax-clogged paper towel acts like a squeegee and halves the application time; he wonders whether an actual squeegee would work.

outline.title: Conclusion and next steps
outline.summary: He wraps up, apologises for short videos, and previews upcoming B-3 and B-6 bomber jacket videos.
